warmup.q: A C program asks the kernel for 1 GB of memory with mmap, a system call that hands a program a range of memory, and then never touches any of it. RSS is the memory a program really has in RAM. About how much does its RSS grow?
options: About 512 MB: the kernel fills half of it up front
The call fails unless 1 GB of RAM is free
warmup.why: mmap only writes down a range of addresses the program may use. The kernel finds RAM for each page of it the first time the program touches that page. In the lab box, RSS stayed at 1 MB after reserving 1 GB, and grew to 1,025 MB only after one byte of every page was written. The first option is the tempting one, because the program asked for a gigabyte and got a yes. A yes from mmap is a promise, and the third section shows how the kernel keeps it, one page at a time.

sections.h: Every program gets its own addresses, and a page table maps them to RAM
sections.html:
Let's look at the memory one program sees. Run cat /proc/self/maps in the lab box, and cat lists the memory it can use, as ranges of addresses. (RAM, the computer's working memory, is a long row of bytes, and each byte's number is its address. Addresses are written in hexadecimal, base 16, with the digits 0 to 9 and a to f.) First comes its own code, at aaaac13d0000. Then come a heap, where a program keeps data it creates as it runs, and the C library, code that almost every program shares. Last is a stack, where each function call keeps its local variables, up near fffff8183000.

Those addresses are virtual. Every process (one running program) has its own set. Two processes can keep different data at the same address, and on every read and write, the hardware translates the address into a place in physical RAM.

A hotel handles group bookings the same way. Each tour group's letter says rooms 1 to 40, and the front desk keeps a list for each group that says which real room each number means. Two groups' room 12 are different rooms. And no guest can walk into another group's room, because their group's list doesn't contain it.

Why not let programs use real RAM addresses? Try the simplest version: each program gets a slice of the 8 GB in Docker's Linux system, and its addresses are real RAM addresses. Two programs built to use the same addresses can't both run. A bad pointer (an address that points to the wrong place) in one program overwrites another program's memory, or the kernel's. And a program can't grow its heap if a neighbor sits right after it.

The next try gives each process a base and a limit. The hardware adds the base to every address and refuses any address past the limit. Every program can now start at 0, and none can reach outside its slice. But the slice must be one unbroken run of RAM. A JVM, the program that runs Java code, may grow its heap to 4 GB and run 40 threads that each need a stack. It has to grab one huge chunk up front, and free memory breaks into gaps too small to use.

The design every modern CPU uses cuts both sides into fixed-size pieces. Physical RAM is split into frames, and virtual addresses into pages of the same size: 4 KB in the lab box, 16 KB on an Apple Silicon Mac. Each process has a page table that says which frame holds each of its pages, if any. Any page can live in any frame. So a 1 GB heap needs no unbroken gigabyte, and a process can't touch another's memory, because the other's frames aren't in its table.

An address splits in two. With 4 KB pages, the last three hexadecimal digits of an address are the offset, the position inside the page. Each hexadecimal digit stands for 4 bits (binary digits, 0 or 1), so that's 12 bits, and 2^12 is 4,096, one page. The rest is the page number. 0xffff42401234 is byte 0x234 of virtual page 0xffff42401.

The table can't be a plain array with one entry per page. The lab box's kernel gives each process 48-bit addresses, 256 TB in all. That's 2^36 pages, and at 8 bytes an entry, the array would need 512 GB for every process. So the table is a tree. The 36 bits of page number split into four groups of 9 bits. Each group picks one of 512 entries in one table, and 512 entries of 8 bytes fill exactly one 4 KB page. The root's entry points to a level 1 table, whose entry points to level 2, then level 3, whose entry holds the frame number.

At the hotel, it's a binder with tabs: the first part of the room number picks a tab, the next picks a page behind it, and so on. Tables exist only under addresses the process uses, so a small program needs only a few dozen KB of them. The figure walks one address.

Four lookups in memory for every read and write sounds slow, and it would be. Next, we'll see the shortcut that makes it cheap.

try.title: Page size and a process's regions
steps: On your Mac, in the Terminal app, run getconf PAGESIZE. It prints the size of one page in bytes.

From the labs folder, start the lab box (docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box) and run the block below. /proc/self/maps lists the regions, the ranges of addresses, of whichever process reads it: here, cat itself.
Find the code, the heap, the C library and the stack. Then work out how many 4 KB pages the [heap] line spans: subtract its start from its end.
try.expect:
On the Mac, 16384. In the box (addresses change on every run, because the kernel picks random places for things, which makes attacks harder):

4096
aaaac13d0000-aaaac13d7000 r-xp 00000000 00:60 1051971                    /usr/bin/cat
aaaac13ef000-aaaac13f0000 r--p 0000f000 00:60 1051971                    /usr/bin/cat
aaaac13f0000-aaaac13f1000 rw-p 00010000 00:60 1051971                    /usr/bin/cat
aaaae7e64000-aaaae7e85000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                          [heap]
...
ffff99230000-ffff993ca000 r-xp 00000000 00:60 1055536                    /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6
...
ffff9942e000-ffff99430000 r-xp 00000000 00:00 0                          [vdso]
...
fffff8162000-fffff8183000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                          [stack]

Each line is one region: its start and end address, its permissions (r-xp is code the process may read and run, rw-p is data it may read and write, kept private to it), then the file it comes from, if any. The heap here is 0x21000 bytes, 33 pages. The vDSO, the small piece of kernel code from the first lesson of this track, is a region too.

video.title: Virtual memory: a page-table walk and a page fault

sections.h: The TLB remembers recent translations, and its reach decides what's cheap to touch
sections.html:
Translating through four tables means four extra reads from memory, each waiting for the one before, ahead of every read or write the program asked for. The CPU keeps copies of recently used memory in its caches, small and fast memories on the chip. A read that misses them costs over 100 ns (billionths of a second) in the lab box, as the 1 GB row in the Try it below shows. Paying that four extra times per access would make every program several times slower.

So the CPU keeps a small cache of recent translations, the TLB (translation lookaside buffer): a page number goes in, a frame number comes out, fast enough that a hit adds almost nothing. At the hotel, it's a sticky note on the desk with the last few lookups, so a busy guest doesn't wait for the binder every time. A miss costs a walk, and the walk's reads may themselves come from the CPU caches. Most accesses hit, because programs reuse pages. A loop over one 4 KB page translates it once and hits 4,095 times.

The TLB is small. CPUs have a first-level TLB of a few dozen to a couple of hundred entries, and a second level of a few thousand. What counts is its reach: entries times page size. Two thousand entries of 4 KB pages cover 8 MB. Say the payments program keeps a 64 MB table in memory and looks up a random spot in it for every payment. It misses the TLB on most lookups and pays a walk each time.

The hotel picture breaks here, on the cost of asking. A guest at the desk waits a few seconds and doesn't mind. A TLB miss costs a few dozen nanoseconds, but a program makes billions of accesses, so that small cost decides whether a big table is fast.

The fix is bigger pages. An entry at level 2 of the tree can map a whole 2 MB block directly, a huge page. One TLB entry then covers 512 times as much memory, and the walk is one level shorter. tlb.c visits one cache line (the 64-byte piece the caches move at a time) in every page of a block of memory, in random order. It does it first with 4 KB pages and then with 2 MB pages. Both runs touch exactly the same cache lines, so the caches behave the same, and only the number of translations differs:

buffer    pages(4 KB)   4 KB pages   2 MB pages
    1 MB         256       0.9 ns       0.9 ns
   16 MB        4096      35.9 ns       7.6 ns

At 1 MB, 256 translations fit in the TLB either way. At 16 MB, 4,096 translations don't fit, and 8 do: the same work costs almost five times as much with small pages. From 256 MB up, both runs are slow, because the data no longer fits in the CPU caches either.

Linux offers huge pages two ways. Transparent huge pages (THP) let the kernel use 2 MB pages for large regions on its own, and the lab box's kernel has THP set to always. Reserved huge pages (hugetlbfs) are set aside by an administrator, and the JVM uses them with -XX:+UseLargePages.

Big or small, every page starts out with no RAM behind it. Next, we'll see what happens the first time a program touches one.

try.title: Measure what a TLB miss costs
steps: os/c/l06/tlb.c builds a random chain through one cache line in each page of a block of memory, then follows it 20 million times. It runs every size twice, with 4 KB pages and with 2 MB pages. It asks for each through madvise, a system call that gives the kernel hints about a region (MADV_NOHUGEPAGE and MADV_HUGEPAGE).
Predict where the 4 KB column jumps, then run it.
try.expect:
Timings vary with your Mac and with what else Docker's Linux system is doing:

buffer    pages(4 KB)   4 KB pages   2 MB pages
    1 MB         256       0.9 ns       0.9 ns
   16 MB        4096      35.9 ns       7.6 ns
   64 MB       16384      49.5 ns      18.0 ns
  256 MB       65536     123.1 ns      78.2 ns
 1024 MB      262144     193.4 ns     139.5 ns

The 4 KB column jumps between 1 MB and 16 MB, where 4,096 translations stop fitting in the TLB. The 2 MB column needs only 8 entries for 16 MB. At 256 MB and 1 GB, both columns are slow, because the data itself misses the CPU caches, and the gap that remains is the cost of the walks.

sections.h: A page fault: the kernel fills in the table on first touch
sections.html:
mmap, the system call that asks the kernel for a range of memory, returns in microseconds for 1 GB. And the process's RSS (resident set size: the part of its memory actually in RAM) doesn't move. The kernel didn't find 262,144 free frames and fill in a quarter of a million table entries. It wrote down one region: this range of addresses is valid, readable and writable, and backed by nothing yet. Regions are what /proc/<pid>/maps lists. The table entries stay empty. At the hotel, the booking is confirmed, and not one room has been made up.

The first time the program writes to a page, the TLB misses, the walk finds an empty entry, and the CPU can't finish the instruction. It raises a page fault: a jump into the kernel that the hardware makes on its own when an instruction can't go on. The kernel's fault handler looks the address up in the process's regions. If the address is inside a writable region, the kernel takes a free frame, fills it with zeros, writes its number into the table and returns. The CPU runs the faulting instruction again, and this time it works. The program notices nothing, except the time it took. It's the guest opening the door of room 12 for the first time, and the room being made up in the moment before they step in.

This is demand paging: mmap promises the memory, and the kernel delivers it one page at a time, on first touch. In the lab box, each fault costs about 0.5 to 1.6 µs (millionths of a second), and touching 1 GB of 4 KB pages takes 262,144 of them. With 2 MB pages, the same gigabyte takes 512. The stepper walks through one fault.

A fault the kernel can settle from RAM, such as a fresh zeroed page or a file's page that's already in memory, is a minor fault. A fault that has to wait for the disk is a major fault. That's a file's page that isn't in memory yet, or a page that was swapped out (written to disk to free its RAM). It costs a disk read: around 0.1 ms on an SSD, the flash drive in most computers, and more on a disk reached over the network. /usr/bin/time -v, a tool that reports what a program used as it ran, and ps -o min_flt,maj_flt both count the two kinds. Minor faults are mostly a cost of starting up and growing. Major faults while a program is busy with real work mean delays.

If the address is in no region, there's nothing to fill in. The kernel sends the thread SIGSEGV, a segmentation fault. (A signal is a message the kernel sends to a process; Processes: fork, exec, wait and signals met them.) At the hotel, it's a guest asking for room 99 of a 40-room booking. The JVM uses this on purpose. Compiled Java code reads through a reference without checking for null first, and when the read faults near address 0, the JVM's signal handler turns the SIGSEGV into a NullPointerException.

That's enough to read the two numbers from the opening. Next, we'll see what a JVM does with all of this.

frames.say: A bug reads through a null pointer, address 0. The walk fails and the kernel looks for a region, as before, but no region covers address 0, so there's nothing to fill in. The kernel sends the thread SIGSEGV, a segmentation fault. The JVM makes this happen on purpose: compiled code reads through a reference without checking for null, and if the read faults near address 0, the JVM's signal handler turns the SIGSEGV into a NullPointerException.

try.title: Count the faults for 1 GB
steps: os/c/l06/touch.c reserves 1 GB with mmap, then writes one byte in every 4 KB page and counts its own page faults. none touches nothing, and huge asks for 2 MB pages.
Predict the fault count and RSS for each of the three runs. The last line runs it under /usr/bin/time -v, which counts the faults from outside the program.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/touch os/c/l06/touch.c /tmp/touch 1024 none /tmp/touch 1024 4k /tmp/touch 1024 huge /usr/bin/time -v /tmp/touch 1024 4k 2>&1 | grep -E "Major|Minor|Maximum resident"

try.expect:
Addresses and timings differ between runs:

reserved 1024 MB at 0xffff5fe00000, page size 4096 bytes, RSS 1 MB, page tables 44 KB
touched (none): 3 page faults in 0 ms, RSS 1 MB, page tables 44 KB
reserved 1024 MB at 0xffff62c00000, page size 4096 bytes, RSS 1 MB, page tables 40 KB
touched (4k): 262147 page faults in 129 ms (0.49 us each), RSS 1025 MB, page tables 2092 KB
reserved 1024 MB at 0xffff65200000, page size 4096 bytes, RSS 1 MB, page tables 44 KB
touched (huge): 515 page faults in 79 ms, RSS 1025 MB, page tables 2096 KB
	Maximum resident set size (kbytes): 1049880
	Major (requiring I/O) page faults: 0
	Minor (reclaiming a frame) page faults: 262216

Reserving costs nothing. Touching 1 GB costs one fault per 4 KB page: 262,144, plus 3 from printf, the C function that prints. The 512 new last-level tables add 2 MB of page tables. With 2 MB pages, it's 512 faults (plus 3). The page tables don't shrink: Linux keeps a spare table for each huge page, so it can split it back into 4 KB pages later. Major faults: 0, because nothing came from disk.

refs.title: OSTEP chapter 21: Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms

aside.title: Why does the kernel fill every new page with zeros?
aside.html: Because the frame may have been someone else's a moment ago. RAM is reused: a frame that one process gives back goes into a pool, and the next process to take a fault gets it. Without the zeros, a program could read another program's old data, a password or a card number among it. Zeroing is also a large part of what a first touch costs, as the comparison of 4 KB and 2 MB pages shows.

sections.h: The JVM reserves gigabytes and touches megabytes
sections.html:
A JVM started with -Xmx4g reserves 4 GB of addresses at start-up for its heap, where Java keeps its objects, the same way touch.c reserved its gigabyte. (-Xmx4g means a heap of at most 4 GB.) Here's one, a small demo standing in for the opening's payments program, as ps shows it in KB:

  PID    VSZ   RSS COMMAND
   40 7304252 181196 java

VSZ (virtual size) is the total size of all the process's regions: 7.3 GB here. That's the 4 GB heap plus other reserved regions. Among them are the thread stacks, 2 MB each, from Threads, and how the JVM maps them to the OS. There's also the code cache, where the JVM keeps Java code it has turned into machine instructions, and its notes about each class. RSS is what's in RAM: 181 MB. At the hotel, VSZ is the rooms booked, and RSS is the rooms made up and in use.

VSZ is what the process could touch. RSS is what it has touched and still holds. A container's memory limit counts pages in RAM, never reserved addresses. Memory allocation: malloc, arenas and why RSS grows, lesson 8 of this track, takes apart what fills the rest of RSS.

Reserved isn't used. Watch RSS, not VSZ.

The heap fills in by demand paging, like everything else. The JVM faults in each heap page the first time it puts objects there. So a fresh JVM pays for its faults during its first minutes of work, a few at a time. -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch makes it touch every heap page at start-up instead. Try it with -Xms1g -Xmx1g, a heap that starts at 1 GB and stays there. Maximum RSS goes from 179 MB to 1,115 MB, because the whole heap is in RAM before main runs.

Minor faults go from about 5,100 to anywhere between 7,900 and 56,000, across several runs. That's well under the 262,144 that 4 KB pages would need, because this kernel gives parts of the heap 2 MB pages. (The -Xmx4g run had 137 MB of AnonHugePages.) How much it gave changed from run to run. Start-up stayed around 0.04 s. The JVM touches the heap in 4 MB chunks, on several threads of its garbage collector (the part that frees memory no longer used) at once. The run used 0.08 to 0.10 s of time in the kernel within 0.04 s on the clock.

Turn on AlwaysPreTouch for long-running programs that need steady response times: the faults happen once, before the first request. It also proves the memory is there. In a container limited to 300 MB, -Xms400m started and ran fine, because it touched little of its heap. With -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch added, the kernel killed it at start-up. Its exit code, the number a program leaves behind when it ends, was 137: 128 plus 9, the number of SIGKILL, as Processes: fork, exec, wait and signals explained. The container's memory.events file, where the kernel counts what happened to the container's memory, said oom_kill 1. Better to find out there, at once, than hours later, when traffic finally grows the heap into the limit. The price is that RSS is the whole heap from the first second.

Last, page size isn't the same everywhere. The lab box's arm64 kernel uses 4 KB pages, and macOS on Apple Silicon uses 16 KB. Code that rounds to pages, or works out how many pages a buffer spans, should ask the system (getconf PAGESIZE) instead of assuming 4096.

So far, every page has belonged to one process, and every page asked for got RAM when touched. Next, we'll see the kernel share pages between processes, and promise more memory than it has.

try.title: VSZ, RSS and AlwaysPreTouch in a JVM
steps: Idle is a small Java program that fills 64 MB with arrays and then waits. Start it with -Xmx4g and compare VSZ with RSS. /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup adds up the process's memory, and its AnonHugePages line is the part in 2 MB pages.
Then start it twice with a 1 GB heap, without and with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch, and predict how maximum RSS and the fault count change.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l06/demo/Idle.java java -Xmx4g -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l06.demo.Idle 20 & pid=$! sleep 3 ps -o pid,vsz,rss,comm -p $pid grep -E "^(Rss|AnonHugePages)" /proc/$pid/smaps_rollup kill $pid for flag in -XX:-AlwaysPreTouch -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch; do echo "== $flag" /usr/bin/time -v java -Xms1g -Xmx1g $flag -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l06.demo.Idle 0 2>&1 | grep -E "Elapsed|Minor|Maximum resident" done

try.expect:
pid 40 holds 64 MB of arrays
  PID    VSZ   RSS COMMAND
   40 7304252 181196 java
Rss:              181196 kB
AnonHugePages:    137216 kB
== -XX:-AlwaysPreTouch
	Elapsed (wall clock) time (h:mm:ss or m:ss): 0:00.04
	Maximum resident set size (kbytes): 178836
	Minor (reclaiming a frame) page faults: 5113
== -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
	Elapsed (wall clock) time (h:mm:ss or m:ss): 0:00.04
	Maximum resident set size (kbytes): 1115084
	Minor (reclaiming a frame) page faults: 41066

7.3 GB reserved, 181 MB in RAM, and 137 MB of that in 2 MB pages. With pre-touch, the JVM holds the whole 1 GB heap before main runs. The fault count moves between runs (from about 7,900 to 56,000 across several runs), depending on how much of the heap gets 2 MB pages.

opening:
Picture the person who looks after the café's payments program, checking on it one morning. They run ps, a command that lists the programs running on a computer. Next to the payments program are two numbers about its memory, in kilobytes: 7,304,252 and 181,196. That's 7.3 GB and 181 MB. The computer has 8 GB of memory in all.

Which one is the program's memory? It's easy to trust the bigger number. It sounds alarming, and it's labelled as the program's size. Someone who trusts it might take memory away from a perfectly healthy program.

In Locks at the OS level: futexes and deadlock, threads shared data in memory. In this lesson, we'll see what an address in memory really is: how each program gets addresses of its own, how the hardware turns them into places in RAM quickly, and why memory you ask for costs nothing until you touch it. Then the two numbers will make sense. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a payments program that showed 7.3 GB in one column and 181 MB in the other, on a computer with 8 GB. The first number is every address it has reserved, its whole heap included. The second is the pages it has touched, the only ones that hold RAM.

In the Terminal app on your Mac, ps -o vsz,rss,comm -p $$ shows both numbers for your own shell, in KB. On the Mac this lesson was written on, it showed about 466 GB reserved and 3.5 MB in RAM.

Next, we'll see how the kernel copies a 512 MB program without copying it, and what happens when it has promised more memory than it has.

compare.title: Touching 1 GB with 4 KB pages and with 2 MB pages

a.label: 4 KB pages (MADV_NOHUGEPAGE)
a.title: touch.c 1024 4k
a.html:
reserved 1024 MB at 0xffff62c00000, page size 4096 bytes, RSS 1 MB, page tables 40 KB
touched (4k): 262147 page faults in 129 ms (0.49 us each), RSS 1025 MB, page tables 2092 KB

b.label: 2 MB pages (MADV_HUGEPAGE)
b.title: touch.c 1024 huge
b.html:
reserved 1024 MB at 0xffff65200000, page size 4096 bytes, RSS 1 MB, page tables 44 KB
touched (huge): 515 page faults in 79 ms, RSS 1025 MB, page tables 2096 KB

compare.note: The same gigabyte of RAM either way. Huge pages need 512 faults instead of 262,144, but the time doesn't drop by the same factor, because most of it goes to filling 1 GB with zeros, which both runs must do. The big win comes later, in the TLB: 16 MB of this memory needs 4,096 translations with small pages and 8 with huge ones. getconf PAGESIZE still says 4096 in both runs, because huge pages are an extra size the kernel uses for some regions, not a new basic page size.

worked.title: Read a JVM's memory from outside the JVM

steps.say: Start with the two totals. VSZ is reserved addresses, and RSS is pages in RAM. min_flt and maj_flt add the counts of minor and major faults. A big gap between VSZ and RSS is normal for a JVM.
steps.code: ps -o pid,vsz,rss,min_flt,maj_flt,comm -p $pid # PID VSZ RSS MINFL MAJFL COMMAND # 40 7304252 179640 5913 0 java

steps.say: Split RSS into anonymous memory (memory that doesn't come from a file: the heap, the stacks and other working memory) and file pages (the JDK's code and libraries, mapped from files on disk). VmPTE adds the size of the page tables themselves.
steps.code: grep -E '^(VmSize|VmRSS|RssAnon|RssFile|VmPTE)' /proc/$pid/status # VmSize: 7304252 kB # VmRSS: 179640 kB # RssAnon: 157792 kB # RssFile: 21848 kB # VmPTE: 692 kB

steps.say: Check how much of it sits in huge pages. With THP set to always, a JVM heap often gets 2 MB pages without asking.
steps.code: cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled # [always] madvise never grep AnonHugePages /proc/$pid/smaps_rollup # AnonHugePages: 137216 kB

steps.say: Read the faults. MINFL (5,913 at start-up) counts first touches: expected while the heap grows, and quiet once it has. MAJFL above 0 and climbing during steady work means pages are coming from disk: a file mapped into memory that isn't cached, or swap. That's the number worth an alert.
steps.code: watch -n 5 ps -o min_flt,maj_flt,rss -p $pid

lab.title: Build a page-table walker with a TLB
steps: Open touch-1g.txt: real output of this lesson's touch.c from the lab box. The tests replay that run on your model and compare the fault count and the size of the page tables.
Read Paging.kt. The constants, Region, Outcome and the Mmu counters are written for you. Mmu is a pretend memory unit, the part of the CPU that translates addresses.
Run the tests once from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All nine fail for now.
Write Paging.split: shift and mask, four times for the indices and once for the offset.
Write PageTable.lookup and map. map creates a Table wherever an entry is empty, and counts it in tables.
Write the Tlb: an LRU cache of capacity translations, one that throws out the least recently used entry when it's full.
Write Mmu.access: the TLB first, then the walk, then a fault or a segfault. Then look at the cliff test: a 64-entry TLB serves a loop over 64 pages perfectly, and a loop over 65 pages not at all.
hints: The index for level l (0 is the root) is ((va ushr (12 + 9 * (3 - l))) and 511).toInt(). ushr shifts the bits right, and and 511 keeps the lowest 9. The offset is (va and 4095).toInt().

object : LinkedHashMap<Long, Long>(16, 0.75f, true) { override fun removeEldestEntry(eldest: MutableMap.MutableEntry<Long, Long>) = size > capacity } is a complete LRU cache: true orders the entries by use, and the override throws out the oldest.
In access, count a fault or a segfault as a TLB miss too, and add Paging.LEVELS to walkReads on every miss.
The model's 516 tables are 2,064 KB. The real run grew by 2,052 KB, because the process already had a root and a level 1 table before mmap.

drill.title: Split an address by hand
drill.prompt: Split 0x0000_7f3a_1234_5678 into its four 9-bit table indices and its 12-bit offset, as Kotlin you could run. Then say how many page faults touching 256 MB costs with 4 KB pages, and with 2 MB pages.

answer.html: val va = 0x0000_7f3a_1234_5678L val indices = (0 until 4).map { level -> ((va ushr (39 - 9 * level)) and 511).toInt() } val offset = (va and 4095).toInt() println(indices) // [254, 232, 145, 325] println(offset.toString(16)) // 678 // 256 MB / 4 KB = 65,536 faults; 256 MB / 2 MB = 128 faults

recap: Every process has its own virtual addresses. Its page table maps each virtual page (4 KB in the lab box, 16 KB on Apple Silicon) to a frame of real RAM; the low 12 bits of an address are the offset inside the page.
The table is a tree: four levels of 512-entry tables, 9 bits of the address each, so a 256 TB range of addresses needs tables only where something is mapped.
The TLB keeps recent translations. Its reach is entries times page size, and past it, every access pays a walk of four reads. 2 MB huge pages multiply the reach by 512.

mmap only records a region. The first touch of each page is a page fault, which the kernel settles with a zeroed frame: a minor fault. A major fault waits for the disk, and an address in no region gets SIGSEGV.
VSZ is reserved addresses, RSS is pages in RAM. A JVM reserves its whole -Xmx up front and faults the heap in as it uses it, unless -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch touches it all at start-up.
The limit: in this lesson, every page belongs to one process, and every page asked for gets RAM on first touch. Real systems share pages between processes, and promise more memory than they have.

explain.prompt: A friend sees a Java program started with -Xmx8g showing a VSZ of 11 GB and an RSS of 900 MB. They ask which number is real, and what -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch would change. Explain it to them.
explain.answer: Both are real, but they measure different things. At start-up, the JVM reserves addresses for the whole 8 GB heap, plus thread stacks, the code cache and its notes about classes, and VSZ adds up every reserved region: 11 GB. Reserving costs no RAM. The kernel gives a page RAM only the first time it's touched: the CPU takes a page fault, and the kernel zeroes a frame and fills in the page table. RSS counts the pages that are really in RAM, 900 MB, and that's the number a container's memory limit and the kernel's out-of-memory killer look at. RSS will grow toward the heap size as the heap gets used. AlwaysPreTouch makes the JVM touch every heap page during start-up. RSS would then be over 8 GB from the first second, all the faults would happen before any work arrives, and if the container's limit can't hold the heap, you'd find out at start-up instead of at the busiest moment of the day.

deeper.html:
Page tables cost memory too. VmPTE in /proc/<pid>/status is the size of a process's page tables. The idle JVM above had 692 KB of them. touch.c went from 44 KB to 2,092 KB after touching 1 GB, which gives a rule of thumb: about 2 MB of tables for every GB of memory mapped with 4 KB pages, 0.2%. A process that maps 100 GB of a file this way spends 200 MB on tables alone, and every process that maps the same file pays it again.

The three settings of THP. The lab box's kernel has THP on for everything:

$ cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
[always] madvise never

With always, any large enough region of anonymous memory can get 2 MB pages, which is why the JVM's heap showed AnonHugePages without asking. With madvise, only regions that ask with madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) get them; touch.c huge and the JVM's -XX:+UseTransparentHugePages both ask that way. A kernel thread, khugepaged, also scans memory and later merges runs of 4 KB pages into 2 MB pages. Huge pages make the TLB's reach much larger. Their costs are memory (a region that touches one byte in a 2 MB block holds all 2 MB) and occasional pauses while the kernel finds or assembles a free 2 MB block.

Files are the other big source of faults. A program can also mmap a file, which lesson 7 of this track covers. The pages of a file mapping come from the page cache, the kernel's copy of file data in memory (lesson 9). If the page is in the cache, the fault is minor, and the kernel only has to map it. If not, the fault is major and waits for the disk. Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages for other programs, relies on this for its index files, and so do many databases. That's why a cold page cache after a restart shows up as a burst of major faults.

sources.title: Memory Layout on AArch64 Linux (kernel documentation)
